new_candidates.body:
On a mechanism closed by many weld constraints, CENIC's cost per step grows as nv³, while SAP's grows as about nv². The number of steps CENIC takes doesn't grow with the model at all, so all of the growth is in the cost of each step. At 207 degrees of freedom, a CENIC step costs 26 times as much as a SAP step. At that size and its default accuracy, CENIC takes 3 to 7 times as long as SAP with 1 ms steps, which reaches similar accuracy, and 130 to 150 times as long as SAP with 50 ms steps.

A profile puts about 90% of CENIC's time in two functions of the weld constraint pool. For each weld, `PrecomputeHessianBlocks()` forms three dense nv×nv blocks, and it does so about six times per step. `AccumulateHessian()` then adds all of them into the Hessian at every Newton iteration. Factoring the Hessian takes only 1.4%.

### The model

This is the unassembled Strandbeest example on [`sherm1/drake` branch `strandbeest_unassembled`](https://github.com/sherm1/drake/tree/strandbeest_unassembled) (commit [41cc537328](https://github.com/sherm1/drake/commit/41cc53732830275cd1d36db2facb7f139354ae77), on master 1217c721d5). PR #25279 It builds Theo Jansen's linkage from unassembled parts:

- **Legs:** each leg is four bars and two rigid triangles, pinned together, forming three kinematic loops. `MultibodyPlant` closes each loop automatically by splitting a link and adding a weld constraint. Each leg adds 10 degrees of freedom (7 parts plus 3 shadow links) and 3 welds.
- **Mobility:** the mechanism is planar, so 3 of each weld's 6 equations are redundant. The 9 independent equations per leg leave it 1 degree of freedom, its crank.
- **One tree:** all legs hang from a single chassis through a single crankshaft, so the whole machine is one kinematic tree, and one clique.

Every run simulates two phases. The models with 8 or more legs stand and walk; the ones with 1, 2 and 4 legs can't stand, so their chassis stays locked and their legs walk in the air.

1. **Crank turning, 1.67 s:** the chassis and crankshaft are locked. A PD motor on each crank (Kp = 1000, Kd = 20) turns it to its phase along a smooth path. There's no contact. (For the one-leg model, the phase is zero, so this is just 0.1 s of settling.)
2. **Walking, 2 s:** the cranks are locked, and a velocity servo turns the crankshaft at 2 rad/s. The feet touch the ground only for the 8- to 20-leg models.

### Problem size

| Model | Legs | Degrees of freedom (nv) | Closed loops | Weld constraints | Weld equations (6 per weld) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| JansenLeg | 1 | 17 | 3 | 3 | 18 |
| TwoLegs | 2 | 27 | 6 | 6 | 36 |
| FourLegs | 4 | 47 | 12 | 12 | 72 |
| EightLegs | 8 | 87 | 24 | 24 | 144 |
| TwelveLegs | 12 | 127 | 36 | 36 | 216 |
| SixteenLegs | 16 | 167 | 48 | 48 | 288 |
| TwentyLegs | 20 | 207 | 60 | 60 | 360 |

### Results

All times are wall-clock seconds per simulated second, the better of two runs, with visualization off. The four columns are:

- **SAP 1 ms:** discrete SAP with a 1 ms time step.
- **SAP 50 ms:** discrete SAP with a 50 ms time step.
- **CENIC 1e-4:** CENIC at its default accuracy, 1e-4.
- **CENIC 1e-2:** CENIC with `--simulator_accuracy=1e-2`.

**Crank turning (no contact)**

| Legs | nv | SAP 1 ms | SAP 50 ms | CENIC 1e-4 | CENIC 1e-2 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 17 | 0.26 | 0.007 | 0.020 | 0.011 |
| 2 | 27 | 0.39 | 0.008 | 0.077 | 0.012 |
| 4 | 47 | 0.68 | 0.014 | 0.28 | 0.047 |
| 8 | 87 | 1.5 | 0.031 | 1.5 | 0.25 |
| 12 | 127 | 2.9 | 0.060 | 4.9 | 0.83 |
| 16 | 167 | 4.9 | 0.10 | 12.5 | 2.1 |
| 20 | 207 | 7.8 | 0.16 | 23.7 | 4.1 |

**Walking (contact for 8 or more legs)**

| Legs | nv | SAP 1 ms | SAP 50 ms | CENIC 1e-4 | CENIC 1e-2 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 17 | 0.26 | 0.005 | 0.033 | 0.004 |
| 2 | 27 | 0.37 | 0.008 | 0.11 | 0.013 |
| 4 | 47 | 0.65 | 0.013 | 0.43 | 0.052 |
| 8 | 87 | 2.3 | 0.076 | 5.0 | 0.73 |
| 12 | 127 | 4.3 | 0.19 | 15.5 | 2.1 |
| 16 | 167 | 7.4 | 0.35 | 39.6 | 5.3 |
| 20 | 207 | 11.4 | 0.60 | 79.0 | 10.2 |

**Cost per step, crank turning**

| Legs | nv | SAP ms/step | CENIC 1e-4 ms/step | CENIC 1e-4 ms per Newton iteration | CENIC ÷ SAP, per step |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 17 | 0.26 | 0.29 | 0.10 | 1.1 |
| 2 | 27 | 0.39 | 0.65 | 0.21 | 1.7 |
| 4 | 47 | 0.68 | 2.4 | 0.76 | 3.5 |
| 8 | 87 | 1.5 | 12.3 | 3.9 | 8.2 |
| 12 | 127 | 2.9 | 41.7 | 13.3 | 14 |
| 16 | 167 | 4.9 | 106 | 33.8 | 22 |
| 20 | 207 | 7.8 | 201 | 64.2 | 26 |

- **CENIC's step count is flat:** for every model with 2 to 20 legs, CENIC turns the cranks in exactly 197 steps and 618 Newton iterations at 1e-4, and in 24 steps and 105 iterations at 1e-2.
- **Scaling:** fitting the 8- to 20-leg models gives a cost per step proportional to nv^3.0 to nv^3.3 for CENIC (at either accuracy, crank turning or walking) and nv^1.9 for SAP.
- **Walking:** CENIC takes 9 to 10 Newton iterations per step at 1e-4, and 15 to 18 at 1e-2, with the same nv³ growth.

**Accuracy**, from the 8- to 20-leg models after 2 s of walking:

| | SAP 1 ms | SAP 50 ms | CENIC 1e-4 | CENIC 1e-2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance walked | 0.84–0.88 m | 0.59–0.64 m | 0.84–0.88 m | 0.69–0.88 m |
| Loop closure error | 2e-6 – 1e-5 m | 4 – 5 mm | 5e-8 – 4e-6 m | 1e-5 – 1.3e-4 m |

SAP at 1 ms and CENIC at 1e-4 agree. SAP at 50 ms still walks, but it walks noticeably less far.

### Charts

Each chart shows the wall-clock time for a whole run (1.67 s of crank turning plus 2 s of walking), plotted against degrees of freedom for the 4- to 20-leg models, whose nv values are evenly spaced. The 4-leg model walks in the air; the others walk on the ground.

```mermaid
xychart-beta
  title "SAP: time step 1 ms (upper), 50 ms (lower)"
  x-axis "degrees of freedom (legs)" ["47 (4)", "87 (8)", "127 (12)", "167 (16)", "207 (20)"]
  y-axis "wall-clock seconds" 0 --> 200
  line [2.43, 7.03, 13.44, 22.87, 35.76]
  line [0.05, 0.2, 0.48, 0.87, 1.46]
```

```mermaid
xychart-beta
  title "CENIC: accuracy 1e-4 (upper), 1e-2 (lower)"
  x-axis "degrees of freedom (legs)" ["47 (4)", "87 (8)", "127 (12)", "167 (16)", "207 (20)"]
  y-axis "wall-clock seconds" 0 --> 200
  line [1.33, 12.36, 39.11, 100.16, 197.72]
  line [0.18, 1.87, 5.64, 14.17, 27.12]
```

Both charts use the same 0–200 s scale.

### Where CENIC's time goes

I profiled SixteenLegs under CENIC at accuracy 1e-2, with 0.5 s of walking, using callgrind. Collection was limited to `Simulator::AdvanceTo()`, so the profile covers only the simulation. The run made 54 `DoStep()` calls. Instructions by function:

| Function | Share of instructions | Calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| [`HolonomicConstraintsPool<double, 6, WeldConstraintsPool<double>>::PrecomputeHessianBlocks()`](https://github.com/RobotLocomotion/drake/blob/1217c721d5045d3e2c42a4dbf19dd3c94d878d81/multibody/contact_solvers/icf/holonomic_constraints_pool.cc#L146-L271) | 68.6% | 324, about 6 per step |
| ↳ from [`IcfModel::SetSparsityPattern()`](https://github.com/RobotLocomotion/drake/blob/1217c721d5045d3e2c42a4dbf19dd3c94d878d81/multibody/contact_solvers/icf/icf_model.cc#L395-L433) | 53.0% | 255 |
| ↳ from [`IcfModel::UpdateTimeStep()`](https://github.com/RobotLocomotion/drake/blob/1217c721d5045d3e2c42a4dbf19dd3c94d878d81/multibody/contact_solvers/icf/icf_model.cc#L575-L577) | 15.6% | 69 |
| The same pool's `AccumulateHessian()`, every Newton iteration | 20.8% | |
| `BlockSparseCholeskySolver::Factor()` | 1.4% | |

Note: `memset()` is 22% of the total, inside the functions above. Almost all of it zero-fills the destinations of the dense `Jᵀ⋅(G⋅J)` products.

`SetSparsityPattern()` runs in `IcfBuilder::UpdateModel()`, twice per step. Because this model has locked joints, it also runs on the reduced model before every solve ([`cenic_integrator.cc`](https://github.com/RobotLocomotion/drake/blob/1217c721d5045d3e2c42a4dbf19dd3c94d878d81/multibody/cenic/cenic_integrator.cc#L556-L563)), three times per step.

The cost is cubic for this reason:

1. Every moving link is in one clique of nv degrees of freedom.
2. For each weld, `PrecomputeHessianBlocks()` forms `H_BB = J_WBᵀ⋅G_Bp⋅J_WB`, `H_AA`, and the cross term as dense nv×nv matrices from 6×nv Jacobians.
3. `AccumulateHessian()` adds all three into the Hessian at every Newton iteration.

That is O(n_welds⋅nv²) work and memory traffic, repeated several times per step, and n_welds grows with nv. Yet each Jacobian has nonzeros only in the columns of the mobilizers on its body's path to the root: about ten here, of up to 207.

### Possible improvements

These are untested ideas.

- **Exploit the Jacobians' tree sparsity:** form each weld's blocks only over the columns on the paths of its two bodies. That makes the cost per weld independent of nv.
- **Don't recompute when only the time step changes:** the weld pool's `G` is `R⁻¹⋅I`, so the time step enters the blocks only through one scalar per weld. `UpdateTimeStep()` could rescale the blocks instead of recomputing them.
- **Reuse the full model's blocks for the reduced model:** the reduced model could take its blocks from the full model's rather than recomputing them before every solve.

### Reproducing

Release build (`-c opt`, GCC 13), Ubuntu 24.04, Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 at 2.2 GHz.

<details><summary>Timing patch and commands</summary>

The timings come from this patch to the example, which prints the problem size and times each phase's `AdvanceTo()`. It also adds `--novisualize`, so that Meshcat publishing doesn't count as solver time and doesn't limit CENIC's step sizes.


### Description

As part of #4178, integration tests using the deprecated `test::Relay` mock system are being refactored to use `Server::EcmScope()`.

In `test/integration/contact_system.cc`, the test `ResetRestoresEarlyContacts` registers a `test::Relay` system solely to record contacts from the ECM on every post-update into a shared `msgs::Contacts` object. It then uses `test::StepUntil` to wait until `validMultipleCollisionContacts()` returns true.

Instead of registering an unnecessary mock relay system and saving state on every post-update, the test predicate inside `test::StepUntil` can take `server.EcmScope()` directly after each step, extract contacts using the existing `contactsFromEcm()` helper, and validate them. This completely eliminates the `test::Relay` mock system and cleans up unused headers (`Relay.hh`, `MockSystem.hh`).

### Tasks
- [ ] Refactor `ResetRestoresEarlyContacts` in `test/integration/contact_system.cc` to use `server.EcmScope()`.
- [ ] Remove `#include "../helpers/Relay.hh"` and unused `#include "plugins/MockSystem.hh"`.
new_candidates.title: Refactor contact_system integration test to use EcmScope

new_candidates.body: CloudXRKit iOS: stream does not cover the full screen height in portrait on iPhone ### Describe the bug On an iPhone in portrait, the CloudXR stream covers the full width of the view but only about 89% of its height. On an iPhone 16 Pro Max (1320 × 2868 px) the streamed image is 2550 px tall; the top 174 px and bottom 144 px show only the ARKit camera feed, with no streamed pixels. The streamed area is roughly centred and its edges are slightly soft (about 2 px). Landscape on the same phone, in the same session, is fully covered. Two iPads running the same app build are fully covered in both orientations (see System Info). ### Steps to reproduce 1. Build an iOS client with CloudXRKit: a RealityKit `ARView` filling the screen (safe areas ignored), with `CloudXRSessionComponent` on an entity under a world `AnchorEntity`. 2. Configure the session with `resolutionPreset = .standardPreset` and connect to an Omniverse Kit server. 3. Hold an iPhone 16 Pro Max in portrait and move close to a large object so the stream fills the frame. 4. Observe bare camera strips at the top and bottom of the screen. 5. Rotate to landscape: the stream covers the whole view. ```swift let arView = ARView(frame: .zero) // laid out full screen, ignoring safe areas let root = AnchorEntity(.world(transform: matrix_identity_float4x4)) let sessionEntity = Entity() sessionEntity.components[CloudXRSessionComponent.self] = .init(session: session) root.addChild(sessionEntity) arView.scene.addAnchor(root) ``` No errors are logged; the session reports Connected and streams normally. ### System Info - Client library: CloudXRKit 6.2.0 (iOS) - Affected: iPhone 16 Pro Max (iPhone17,2), iOS 27.2 (24B119), screen 1320 × 2868 px (about 2.17:1), where the stream is 2550 px tall (about 1.93:1) - Not affected, same app build, both orientations: - iPad mini (A17 Pro), MXN63LL/A, screen 1488 × 2266 px (about 1.52:1) - iPad Pro 12.9-inch (5th generation), MHNH3LL/A, screen 2048 × 2732 px (4:3) - Server: Omniverse Kit 110.4.1, CloudXR Runtime version, e.g. 6.0.8 - Server OS: Windows 11 - GPU: e.g. RTX 6000 Ada - GPU Driver: 597.16 - Commit / Isaac Sim Version / CUDA: not applicable (Kit application, not Isaac Sim) ### Additional context What we ruled out: - **Not safe-area layout.** The gaps (174 px top, 144 px bottom) do not match the device's safe-area insets (186 px top, 102 px bottom). - **Probably not a pixel-height cap.** Setting the `ARView`'s `contentScaleFactor` to 2 (880 × 1912 px drawable) left the gap essentially unchanged (top strip 157 px instead of 174, measured on the 3× screenshot). - **Not orientation handling in the app.** The app has no portrait-specific or aspect-specific code; landscape on the same device is correct. - **The limit sits between 1.52:1 and 2.17:1.** A 1.52:1 portrait screen (iPad mini) is fully covered; on the 2.17:1 iPhone the stream stops at about 1.93:1. This looks like a limit on vertical field of view or on the width-to-height aspect ratio of the streamed frame. The iOS `ResolutionPreset` enum exposes only `standardPreset`, and we found no public frame-size or field-of-view setting on the client. Screenshots attached: portrait at 3× scale and at 2× scale, zoomed in on a large dark object so the uncovered strips are easy to see. ### Checklist - [ ] I have checked that there is no similar issue in the repo (**required**) - [ ] I have checked that the issue is not in running Isaac Sim itself and is related to the repo ### Acceptance Criteria - [ ] In portrait on an iPhone (about 2.17:1 screen), the stream covers the full `ARView`, as it does in landscape and on iPad. - [ ] If a field-of-view or aspect-ratio limit is intentional, it is documented and configurable from the client or server.

### Summary
`moveit_ros/moveit_servo/package.xml` has `<exec_depend>` on `moveit_ros_visualization` and `joy` for the demo launch files (`launch/demo_*.launch.py`) and RViz configs (`config/demo_rviz_config*.rviz`).

`servo_node` and `moveit_servo_lib_{cpp,ros}` do not use RViz, Qt, or `joy`, so headless robots depending on `moveit_servo` end up pulling `rviz2`, Qt, OGRE, LLVM, and SDL.

### Proposal
Move the demo executables, `launch/demo_*.launch.py`, and RViz demo configs into a separate `moveit_servo_demos` package (or `moveit2_tutorials`), so `moveit_servo` can drop `moveit_ros_visualization` and `joy` from its `<exec_depend>` list.

If maintainers are on board with this direction, I am happy to work on the PR.
new_candidates.title: Split moveit_servo demos into a separate package to avoid rviz2/joy exec_depends

new_candidates.body:
### Summary
In #2836, `launch_testing_ros` was moved to `<exec_depend>` in `controller_manager/package.xml` so downstream tests importing `controller_manager.test_utils` work. As a result, production deployments of `controller_manager` pull `launch_testing_ros`, `launch_testing`, and `pytest` at runtime even though `ros2_control_node` and `spawner` never import `test_utils`.

### Proposal
Extract `controller_manager.test_utils` into a separate `controller_manager_testing` package (matching the existing `hardware_interface_testing` / `ros2_control_test_assets` pattern) with `<exec_depend>launch_testing_ros</exec_depend>`, and drop `launch_testing_ros` from `controller_manager`'s runtime `<exec_depend>`.

If maintainers are happy with this direction, I am happy to work on the PR.
new_candidates.title: Extract controller_manager.test_utils to drop launch_testing_ros from runtime exec_depend

new_candidates.body:
### Summary
Since #1763, `hardware_interface/package.xml` declares `<exec_depend>sdformat_urdf</exec_depend>`. `hardware_interface` only parses `<sdf>` with `tinyxml2` and delegates to `urdf::Model::initString()` (which loads `sdformat_urdf` via `pluginlib` if present), so URDF-only robots end up pulling `sdformat`, `gz-*`, and Ruby at runtime even though `ros2/urdf` itself does not depend on `sdformat_urdf`.

### Proposal
1. Change `<exec_depend>sdformat_urdf</exec_depend>` to `<test_depend>sdformat_urdf</test_depend>` in `hardware_interface/package.xml` (keeping `TEST_F(TestComponentParser, successfully_parse_valid_sdf)` green).
2. Add `<exec_depend>sdformat_urdf</exec_depend>` to `ros-controls/gz_ros2_control` so SDF/Gazebo users still get it automatically.

If maintainers agree with this approach, I am happy to work on both PRs.
new_candidates.title: Move sdformat_urdf from exec_depend to test_depend in hardware_interface

new_candidates.body:
## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:                                                                                  
    - Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS (inside the ROS container; the host runs Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS)
- Computer:                                                                                          
    - Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, x86_64
- ROS2 Version:                                                                                      
    - Lyrical, apt binaries
- Version or commit hash:
    - ros-lyrical-nav2-graceful-controller  1.5.2-2resolute.20260921.021123
- DDS implementation:
    - rmw_cyclonedds_cpp (ros-lyrical-rmw-cyclonedds-cpp 4.1.5-1resolute.20260915.051853)


#### Steps to reproduce issue
                                                    
Any goal reached within xy tolerance but with a large remaining heading error will enter rotateToTarget(). With these parameters the commanded angular velocity exceeds v_angular_max:

  controller_server:
    ros__parameters:                                                                                   
      FollowPath:
        plugin: nav2_graceful_controller::GracefulController
        v_angular_max: 1.0
        v_angular_min_in_place: 0.25
        rotation_scaling_factor: 1.0

Send a goal at the robot's current position with a heading ~180 deg away, then watch the controller output:
ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel --field angular.z

#### Expected behavior

angular.z never exceeds the configured v_angular_max in either direction.

#### Actual behavior

rotateToTarget() applies only a lower bound:

  vel.angular.z = params_->rotation_scaling_factor * angle_to_target * params_->v_angular_max;
  vel.angular.z = std::copysign(1.0, vel.angular.z) * std::max(
    abs(vel.angular.z),
    params_->v_angular_min_in_place);

std::max can only raise a value, so nothing bounds it from above. The command is rotation_scaling_factor * angle_to_target * v_angular_max, which exceeds v_angular_max whenever |angle_to_target| > 1 / rotation_scaling_factor, independent of v_angular_max, since it appears on both sides. With the default rotation_scaling_factor of 0.5 that is any heading error above 2 rad (114 deg); at 1.0 it is above 1 rad (57 deg).

Measured on a differential-drive robot: angular.z peaked at 2.333 rad/s with v_angular_max set to 1.0.

#### Reproduction instructions

Reproducible as a unit test, no robot required — configure the controller as above and call rotateToTarget(3.0). Expected 1.0, actual 3.0.
new_candidates.title: Graceful controller doesn't obey the max angular velocity param

new_candidates.body:
We currently use the raw twist from the odom smoother in the controller server and other locations [1]. This appears to be a regression from https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/commit/9cd0f9fc977242a30f4921c8fdb99ada2ec61093 which centralized the nav_2d_utils and nav2_utils version of the odom smoother together. This uses the raw current, unsmoothed velocity, which is using a noisy industrial or legged platform creates major jitter / chatter. 


[1] https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Aros-navigation%2Fnavigation2+getRawTwist&type=code
new_candidates.title: Use Twist from the Odom Smoother in Nav2 Controller rather than Raw Twist

new_candidates.body:
## Bug report

### Required Info

* **Operating System**: Ubuntu 24.04 (Docker `ros:jazzy-ros-base`)
* **Computer**: x86_64 Linux (Docker)
* **ROS 2 Version**: ROS 2 Jazzy (`rclcpp` 28.1.22)
* **Navigation2 Version**: `main` branch (94bace6, verified unchanged on `main` 64d5227338 and `lyrical` branch; `kilted`/`jazzy`/`humble` do not have `nav2::Rate` from #6063 and are unaffected)
* **DDS Implementation**: `rmw_fastrtps_cpp`

### Summary

Calling `set_parameters` on `/docking_server` or `/following_server` while a `/dock_robot`, `/undock_robot`, or `/follow_object` action is executing causes a **permanent ABBA deadlock** that freezes both the action worker thread and the node's executor (subsequent parameter/service calls time out and the node cannot exit cleanly on `SIGTERM`).

### Root Cause (Lock-Order Inversion)

1. **`rclcpp` parameter callback holds the node's internal parameters mutex first, then blocks on `param_handler_->mutex_`:**
   - `nav2_util::ParameterHandler::activate()` registers `updateParametersCallback` via `add_post_set_parameters_callback(...)`.
   - `rclcpp::node_interfaces::NodeParameters::set_parameters_atomically()` holds `NodeParameters::mutex_` while invoking parameter callbacks.
   - Unlike `nav2_controller/src/parameter_handler.cpp:194` (which uses non-blocking `mutex_.try_lock()`), both docking and following acquire a **blocking** lock:
     - `nav2_docking/opennav_docking/src/parameter_handler.cpp:104`: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock_reinit(mutex_);`
     - `nav2_following/opennav_following/src/parameter_handler.cpp:113`: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock_reinit(mutex_);`

2. **Action worker holds `param_handler_->mutex_` first, then acquires `NodeParameters::mutex_` via `nav2::Rate`:**
   - `DockingServer::dockRobot()` (`docking_server.cpp:177`) and `undockRobot()` (`:659`) hold `param_handler_->getMutex()` across `nav2::Rate(this, ...)` constructions (`:179`, `:412`, `:438`, `:471`, `:552`, `:584`, `:661`).
   - `FollowingServer::followObject()` (`following_server.cpp:182`) holds `param_handler_->getMutex()` across `nav2::Rate(this, ...)` constructions (`:184`, and `getRefinedPose()` at `:507` during initial wait / retry).
   - `nav2::Rate(node, rate)` (`nav2_ros_common/include/nav2_ros_common/rate.hpp:44-45`) calls `node->get_node_parameters_interface()->has_parameter("use_sim_time")` and `get_parameter("use_sim_time")`, both of which lock `NodeParameters::mutex_`.

**Cycle:**
- **Executor thread**: holds `NodeParameters::mutex_` -> waits for `param_handler_->mutex_` (`updateParametersCallback`)
- **Action worker (`std::async`)**: holds `param_handler_->mutex_` -> waits for `NodeParameters::mutex_` (`nav2::Rate` -> `has_parameter("use_sim_time")`)

### Steps to Reproduce (Plain Non-Sanitizer Build, Stock Defaults)

#### Case 1: `opennav_following` (5/5 reproduced)
1. Launch stock `opennav_following` with `controller.use_collision_detection: false`, static TF `odom -> base_link`, and `/odom` publisher; configure and activate `/following_server`.
2. Send one `/follow_object` goal (`pose_topic: "/detected_dynamic_pose"`, `tracked_frame: ""`, `max_duration: 10s`).
3. Immediately after goal acceptance, send a single parameter update:
   ```bash
   ros2 param set /following_server controller_frequency 45.0
   ```
4. Observe that after the first retry logs `Using last known heading to find object again`, the worker enters `getRefinedPose()` -> `nav2::Rate` (`:507`) and hangs permanently:
   - `ros2 param get /following_server controller_frequency` times out (`rc=124`).
   - On `SIGTERM`, `SimpleActionServer` repeatedly logs `Action callback is still running and missed deadline to stop` and requires `SIGKILL`.
   - **Control (no `set_parameters`)**: all 3 retries complete normally, goal aborts cleanly, and `GetParameters` responds immediately (`0.00s`).

#### Case 2: `opennav_docking` (11/12 reproduced)
1. Launch stock `opennav_docking` with stock default timeouts (`initial_perception_timeout=5.0`, `dock_approach_timeout=30.0`, `max_retries=3`), `SimpleChargingDock` with `use_external_detection_pose: true`, static TF `odom -> base_link`, `/odom`, and external dock pose publisher; configure and activate `/docking_server`.
2. Send one `/dock_robot` goal (`use_dock_id: true`, `dock_id: "test_dock"`, `navigate_to_staging_pose: false`).
3. Immediately after goal acceptance, send a single `SetParameters` request (`controller_frequency=45.0`).
4. In 11/12 trials, the node permanently deadlocks (1 at `doInitialPerception` `:412`, 10 at `resetApproach` `:584`), and independent `GetParameters` requests time out.
   - **Control (no `set_parameters`)**: 2/2 trials stay responsive (`GetParameters` succeeds).

### Expected Behavior

Dynamic parameter updates during an active docking or following action should either be safely rejected or applied without deadlocking the node executor and action worker.

### Suggested Fix Directions

1. **Avoid acquiring `NodeParameters::mutex_` inside `nav2::Rate` (or before locking):**
   - `selectSteadyOrSimClock()` could inspect the node clock type / a cached `use_sim_time` flag instead of querying `get_node_parameters_interface()->has_parameter("use_sim_time")` on every `nav2::Rate` construction; or
2. **Avoid blocking in parameter callbacks / holding `param_handler_->getMutex()` across long action loops:**
   - Reject dynamic updates in `validateParameterUpdatesCallback` (`on_set_parameters_callback`) via `mutex_.try_lock()` returning `result.successful = false` when an action is running (preserving parameter consistency between ROS parameter storage and `params_`, unlike silently skipping inside `post_set_parameters_callback`), or snapshot `params_` under a short lock at action start instead of holding `param_handler_->getMutex()` across the full action execution.
new_candidates.title: [opennav_docking / opennav_following] ABBA deadlock between nav2::Rate in action worker and dynamic set_parameters callback
